name: Outbound link decoration
plain: Adding an ID to a link's URL so the next site can read it and link the visit.
meaning: Meta adds fbclid to outbound clicks; Google's linker adds _gl with first party cookie IDs valid for a short time (about 2 minutes). The next site turns the ID into its own cookie. Safari caps such cookies at 24 hours, Firefox and Brave strip known params.

access.persistence: Parameter valid for the click; resulting cookie 24 h (Safari) to 400 days
access.revocation: Clear site data, browser privacy settings

story.what_it_is: Adding an ID to the end of a link so the next site can recognise you.

marketing.name: Tracking prevention
marketing.pitch: WebKit says Safari limits cookies made from decorated links, since they can be used to follow people.

story.for_you: You click a link in a post or ad, and a code is added to the address. The next site reads it and starts to track you with its own cookie. Safari caps such cookies at a day.
story.for_makers: Meta adds fbclid to outbound clicks, and Google adds _gl to link its own domains. The next site turns the ID into a cookie it controls. That makes tracking work after third party cookies are blocked.

use_cases.example: You click a link in a Facebook post. Meta adds fbclid so the news site can tell the click came from Facebook.
A Google ad adds a gclid to the link, so the store can credit a sale to the exact ad.
A company with two domains adds _gl so Analytics sees one visitor and not two.
A game portal adds an ID to links to an affiliate store, so a purchase is credited.
An influencer link adds a code that tells a shop which creator brought you.
Firefox and Brave strip known IDs from links, which is how they fight the practice.

risks: Link IDs can leak when shared

technical_bounds: Cannot read the other site's cookies
